dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Welcome. You've been described as Kazakhstan's youngest environmental activist. Is that a title you're comfortable with?

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: I'm comfortable with "activist." I don't think age is the most interesting thing about the work.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Tell us how you got started. What first made you interested in environmental issues?

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: I was raised in a village near the Ural River. Every summer I could see that the river was lower than the year before. The fish were disappearing. I asked my grandmother why, and she said things had been better when she was young.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: And when did you decide to become an activist rather than just someone who noticed these things?

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: When I was seventeen, a factory near our village was found to have been releasing untreated chemicals into the river. The water had been contaminated for years. Nobody was being held responsible. That's when I knew I had to do something.

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: Eventually it was shut down and the owners were fined. But the cleanup hasn't been completed — the riverbed is still being studied. It will take years.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: What is your main focus now?

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: Water rights. Communities in rural Kazakhstan are being denied clean water that is legally guaranteed to them. The problem is being documented by our organisation.

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: Young people. More young Kazakhstanis care about the environment than ever before. The attitude has been changed by climate news, by what they can see with their own eyes. That gives me a lot of hope.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: What would you say to a student thinking about environmental work?

dialogue.speaker: Aizhan
dialogue.text: Start local. The issues that have been ignored for decades are right outside your window. Learn the science. Talk to the communities. Then act.

questions.text: "A factory was found to have been releasing chemicals." This uses:
questions.hint: "was found to have been RELEASING" = complex passive + Perfect Continuous. The releasing was ongoing before it was discovered. ✅

questions.text: "Communities are being denied clean water." "are being denied" is:
questions.hint: "are being denied" = Present Continuous Passive (am/is/are + being + past participle). Ongoing denial right now. ✅

questions.text: "The riverbed is still being studied." — "is still being studied" means:
opts: The study is ongoing right now
questions.correct: The study is ongoing right now
questions.hint: "is being studied" = Present Continuous Passive. The studying is happening now and is not finished. ✅

questions.text: "The factory ___ (eventually shut) down and the owners ___ (fine)."
questions.hint: Past Simple Passive. "was SHUT down" / "were FINED." ✅ The factory = singular (was), owners = plural (were).
